name: Rose-Purple
lede: Rose-Purple is a light, bright purple-pink from Ridgway's 1886 color book; the books we hold are silent about it, so this is a short article about where the name comes from.

sections.title: A Ridgway name
sections.body: Rose-Purple was in Ridgway's Nomenclature of Colors of 1886 and reappears on plate XXVI of his 1912 Color Standards [2]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 carried it over and files it under brilliant purple [2]. The name joins [[rose]] and [[purple]] [2]. Close neighbors in hue are [[rosy-pink]] and [[pinky-purple]], both also in our library [2].

sections.title: What the books say
sections.body: Nothing. The only hit in our books is a shirt printed with crimson roses and purple poppies, which is a pattern, not a color term [1]. We found no passage on the color itself, so we say no more about its history [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive has this color covering at least 1% of its canvas, as photographed [3]. That describes this archive, not painting as a whole [3].

origin.named_after: rose and purple (plant word plus color word)

notes.cite: ColorHub library, Rose-Purple: Ridgway 1886 and 1912 plate XXVI; ISCC-NBS 1955 block 222

questions.q: Whose color book first carries the name Rose-Purple in our sources?
True or false: painters in our archive use this color widely.

openers: Rose-Purple has been a named color since at least 1886.

issues: Removed unsupported claim about a nineteenth-century naming habit.
